summary: An April 1st joke memo defining a Management Information Base for drip-type heated beverage hardware, with objects for managing coffee-brewing and maintenance devices. It is humorous and was not meant to be implemented.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st RFC applies SNMP management language to coffee pots. It defines objects for describing a pot and reading its operating status, coffee level, and temperature.

questions: what is the coffee pot mib
subtitle: An April 1st joke defining SNMP management objects for coffee equipment.

tldr.problem: The joke asks what a network-management information base for coffee-brewing hardware might look like.
tldr.mechanism: The COFFEE-POT-MIB defines objects for a pot's name, capacity, brew type, location, status, level, start time, and temperature.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2325 is an April 1st joke and does not specify a real coffee-device management deployment.

today: RFC 2325 is an Informational April 1st joke. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A MIB for Coffee Hardware
sections.content:
RFC 2325 is an April 1st joke formatted as an extension to the SNMPv2 Management Information Base. It defines objects for managing devices that brew, store, and deliver heated coffee beverages.

The memo places the coffee module in a layered interface-management model and describes its relation to other MIB modules. It even notes that using a coffee port as a network interface is unlikely.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC uses real MIB structure to describe fictional network management for coffee equipment. Its serious formatting is part of the joke.

sections.title: The Coffee-Pot Objects
sections.content:
The module defines objects for the pot's vendor description, capacity, brew type, and physical location. It also defines a read-only operating status with values for off, brewing, holding, other, and waiting.

Other objects report the amount of coffee and its unit, the scheduled start time when the pot is waiting, the time since brewing began, and the coffee's ambient temperature in degrees Centigrade. The RFC notes that current hardware prevents changing the pot state through SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects report what kind of pot it is, where it is, whether it is brewing, how much coffee it holds, and its temperature. The text says the pot's operating state cannot be changed through SNMP.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed in the memo.

This brief section sits alongside the document's formal MIB definitions and contributes to its deadpan presentation.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security issues. That short statement is part of its formal, joke specification style.
